title: Berkeley Clubs Research
note: Demo fixture. Illustrative club facts written for the demo — not verified real-world info. Agents may APPEND messages to make this longer/richer (target: feels like an hour of research) but must not alter existing facts, especially the Free Ventures deadline and the Berkeley Consulting rejection, which the demo depends on.

profile.name: Tarun
profile.context: Incoming Berkeley freshman, applied math, CS-focused. Building a startup on the side.
goals: startup and technical exposure over resume-padding
wary of clubs with brutal recruiting processes or huge time commitments

messages.content: I'm an incoming Berkeley freshman doing applied math but really I care about CS, AI, and startups. I want to figure out which clubs to actually go for in the fall. I'd rather join 2 great ones than 5 mediocre ones.

Good constraint. Let's define what 'great' means for you first: do you want clubs that get you building (project/dev clubs), clubs that get you into the startup ecosystem (accelerator/VC-adjacent), or clubs that are mostly social/community?

Building and startup ecosystem. Community matters but as a property of the club, not the point of it. Also I'm already running a startup with a cofounder so time is genuinely limited — maybe 8-10 hrs/week total for clubs.

Noted: builder-first, startup-adjacent, tight-knit, hard cap around 8-10 hours/week across everything. Candidates worth researching: Machine Learning at Berkeley (ML@B), Free Ventures, Codebase, Blueprint, Berkeley Consulting, and the hackathon org scene. Want to go through them one by one?
Yeah let's do it. Start with ML@B.

ML@B: the serious ML org — research-style projects and industry collaborations. Strong technical signal and alumni network. The flip side: selective admissions and a real workload; members describe it as a part-time job during project cycles. Given your 8-10 hour cap while running a startup, it would likely be your ONLY club if you join.
Hmm. Strong maybe. What about Free Ventures? That one sounds most aligned with what I'm already doing.

Free Ventures is Berkeley's student-run startup accelerator — you apply WITH your startup, and if accepted you get structure, mentorship, and demo day exposure. For someone already building, it converts time you're already spending into community and accountability rather than adding a new workload. Key logistics from their fall cycle: applications close September 11, with an info session on September 3.
Ok that's basically perfect for us. What about Codebase?

Codebase does semester-long software projects for real industry clients in small teams. Great engineering experience and a close-knit team structure. But it's a significant fixed commitment on someone else's project — which competes directly with your startup hours rather than compounding them. Good option if you want pure swe reps; redundant if Free Ventures works out.
What about Berkeley Consulting? A friend keeps hyping it.

Berkeley Consulting is prestigious and well-run, but it's consulting: client decks and business analysis, with a famously intense multi-round recruiting process including case-style interviews. Based on everything you've said — builder-first, allergic to heavy recruiting theater — this looks like a poor fit despite the brand.
Yeah, ruling out Berkeley Consulting. Case interviews for a club is exactly what I said I didn't want. What about Blueprint?

Ruled out: Berkeley Consulting (recruiting process mismatch). Blueprint builds software for nonprofits — mission-driven, welcoming culture, moderate commitment. It's the most community-warm option on your list, though the least startup-adjacent. A reasonable second club if your first is Free Ventures rather than ML@B.

Ok so current state of my head: Free Ventures is priority one, then it's ML@B vs Codebase vs Blueprint for the second slot, leaning ML@B if I can survive the workload. Keep all this — I'll come back after I talk to my cofounder about the Free Ventures app.

Saved state: Priority 1 = Free Ventures (apply with the startup; apps close Sept 11, info session Sept 3). Slot 2 = ML@B vs Codebase vs Blueprint — leaning ML@B, workload is the open question against your 8-10 hr/week cap. Ruled out = Berkeley Consulting (case-interview recruiting). Open thread: cofounder conversation before the Free Ventures application.
Before I lock anything in, I want to actually understand ML@B's workload instead of guessing. What does a semester in it actually look like week to week?

Here's the honest shape of it, based on how members describe the cycle.

**Structure.** ML@B runs on semester-long project cycles. You're placed on a project team of roughly 4-6 people, either an internal research project or an industry collaboration where a company brings a real problem and a dataset. Industry projects are the ones people talk about — they come with a real deliverable and a real stakeholder, which is both the appeal and the workload.

**Week-to-week.** A typical week is one team meeting (1-1.5 hrs), one all-org meeting or tech talk (1 hr, semi-optional after your first semester), and then the actual work — which is where the variance lives. Early semester it's 4-6 hrs/week: reading papers, scoping, getting the data pipeline standing up. Mid-semester it settles around 8-10. The last three weeks before the final presentation are where it becomes a part-time job — people report 15-20 hr weeks, occasionally worse if the model isn't converging and the client presentation is Thursday.

**The new-member tax.** Your first semester adds an education track on top of the project: a structured curriculum covering the ML fundamentals the org assumes, with assignments. Budget an extra 3-4 hrs/week for that in fall. So realistically your first semester is the most expensive one, not the cheapest.

**What that means against your cap.** Your 8-10 hrs/week is a hard ceiling across *all* clubs, and you're running a startup on top. ML@B alone would average right at your ceiling and blow through it for a month. If you join ML@B, it is your only club, and there will be weeks where it competes directly with the startup. That's not a reason to rule it out — it's the tradeoff you'd be accepting explicitly.
That's roughly what I feared. What do people actually get out of it though? Trying to figure out if the ceiling-blowing weeks buy something I can't get elsewhere.

Three things, in descending order of how unique they are to ML@B.

**1. The technical signal, which is real.** ML@B has one of the strongest reputations among Berkeley technical orgs, and recruiters at ML-heavy companies know it. That matters less to you than to most people — you're building your own thing, so you're not optimizing for the internship funnel. But it's not nothing: it's a credential that opens conversations, including with investors who use it as a proxy for "this person can actually build."

**2. The peer group.** This is the part that's hardest to replicate. You'd be on a team with people who read papers for fun and have shipped models that do something. For someone whose stated goal is building and technical depth, being surrounded by people slightly ahead of you is the highest-leverage thing on this list. You said community matters as a property of the club rather than the point of it — this is exactly that.

**3. Structured exposure to problems you wouldn't pick.** Industry projects hand you a messy real dataset and a stakeholder with opinions. That's a different muscle from building your own product, where you control the problem definition. Some people find this the most valuable part; others find it frustrating for exactly the same reason.

**What you can get elsewhere:** the ML skills themselves. You can learn the material from courses and from building. What you can't easily buy is the peer group plus the forcing function of a team depending on you.

**The counter-argument you should hold onto:** you already have a forcing function and a technical peer — your cofounder and your startup. ML@B's core value proposition partially duplicates something you already have. That's the strongest case against it, and it's stronger than the workload argument.
Fair. What's the recruiting process like — is it another Berkeley Consulting situation?

No, and the difference matters given what you ruled out.

**ML@B's process** is technical rather than social-performance. Broadly: written application (short answers about background and a project you've built), then a technical interview covering ML fundamentals and some coding, then a behavioral/fit round with current members. Two rounds after the app, not four. Timeline is early-to-mid September with decisions before the end of the month.

**Why it's not the Berkeley Consulting problem.** Your objection there was case interviews — a process that tests performance at a genre of conversation rather than at the actual work. ML@B's interview tests whether you can reason about ML problems, which is the thing the club does. You may or may not pass it, but you won't feel like you're being evaluated on a skill that only exists inside the recruiting process itself.

**Acceptance rate** is low — this is a selective org and the applicant pool is large and strong. Treat it as a real possibility that you don't get in, which is an argument for applying to a second thing rather than betting the fall on it.

**Prep cost:** modest. A weekend of brushing up on fundamentals plus having a clear story about something you've built. You have the second part already — the startup is a better answer to "tell me about a project" than most applicants will have.
Ok. Switch to Codebase — I know less about it.

**Codebase** is a software consulting-style org: semester-long engineering projects for real industry clients, done in small teams. Think of it as the software-building analogue to what Berkeley Consulting does with slide decks.

**Structure.** Teams of roughly 5-6, one client per team per semester. Clients range from startups to established companies. You ship something real that gets used — that's the pitch, and it's a legitimate one. There's a project manager and a tech lead on each team, roles you can grow into by your second or third semester.

**Workload.** More predictable than ML@B, which is its main advantage. Steady 8-10 hrs/week with a fixed weekly team meeting and a sprint cadence. It doesn't have ML@B's brutal three-week spike, because client software projects get scoped down rather than blowing up — the deliverable adjusts. The flip side is that the floor is also higher: there's no light week, because a client is waiting.

**Culture.** Close-knit and well-run, with a genuine social layer. People describe it as one of the friendlier technical orgs.

**The problem for you specifically.** It's a significant *fixed* commitment for someone who already has an unpredictable startup. Codebase's whole value is reliability — a client depends on you shipping on a schedule. If your startup has a launch week or a fundraising sprint, you can't quietly take a light week the way you could in a looser org, because someone external is affected. You'd be signing up for a second set of external obligations on top of the ones you already have.

**And the duplication argument is sharper here than with ML@B.** Codebase teaches you to build software for a real user under a deadline. That is a precise description of what you are already doing with your cofounder, every week, at higher stakes. The marginal learning is smaller than the marginal time cost.
That duplication point is landing. What about the recruiting process for Codebase?

Similar shape to ML@B, slightly lighter.

Written application, then a technical interview (general software engineering — data structures, some practical coding, walking through a project you've built), then a fit round. Also selective, though the technical bar is calibrated to general engineering rather than ML specifically, so it's a wider net.

**Timing note that matters for planning:** Codebase, ML@B, and most technical orgs recruit in the same two-week window in early-to-mid September. This is the actual constraint you should be building around, not the semester workload. You will be doing multiple applications and multiple interviews in the same fortnight — during syllabus week, while running a startup, and while Free Ventures applications are also open and closing September 11.

That's the real scheduling collision in your fall, and it argues for deciding *now* which two things you're applying to, rather than keeping five options open into September and doing all of them badly.
Ok, Blueprint next. You mentioned mission-driven and moderate commitment — I want the actual numbers and the actual downside.

**Blueprint** builds software for nonprofits. Teams of roughly 5-7 take on a nonprofit client for a semester or, more often, for a full year — nonprofit projects tend to run longer because the clients move slower and the scope is fuzzier at the start.

**Workload: 6-8 hrs/week, and it genuinely holds.** This is the least spiky of the three. One weekly team meeting, one weekly org-wide meeting that's more social than mandatory, and development time you largely control. There is no client demo day with a company's VP in the room, so the end-of-semester crunch is real but mild — a demo to the nonprofit's program director rather than a stakeholder presentation.

**Culture is the strongest part.** Blueprint is consistently described as the warmest of the technical orgs. Lower ego, more collaborative, more patient with people who are still learning. If you want the "tight community" property you listed as a goal, Blueprint delivers it more reliably than ML@B or Codebase.

**Recruiting is the lightest of the three.** Application plus a single conversational interview that's more about motivation and fit than technical depth. Highest acceptance rate of the clubs on your list by a wide margin. If your fall strategy needs a safety, this is the natural one.

**Now the downsides, which are real for you specifically.**

*The technical ceiling is lower.* Nonprofit software is usually CRUD-shaped: a donor management dashboard, a volunteer scheduling tool, a data migration off a spreadsheet system. Solid engineering practice, genuinely useful to the client, but you will not be pushed past what you can already do. Compare that to ML@B, where the project might not work at all — which is where the learning is.

*The pace can be frustrating.* Nonprofit clients have small teams and competing priorities. Weeks disappear waiting on a stakeholder to answer a question about requirements. For someone used to startup velocity, this is the most commonly cited source of frustration.

*Duplication again, in a milder form.* You already build software. Blueprint's marginal technical contribution is close to zero for you. What it adds is community and a different kind of user — a nonprofit program manager is not a technical user, and building for non-technical users is a skill worth having.

**Honest summary:** Blueprint is the right answer if what you want from a second club is people and a low-variance commitment. It is the wrong answer if what you want is to be pushed technically. Given your stated goals lean builder-first and technical, Blueprint is the "safe but slightly off-target" option — which is exactly why it keeps showing up in your slot-2 consideration rather than winning it.
Good. Now go deep on Free Ventures since that's my priority one. What do they actually look for, what does the application involve, and what does the semester look like if I get in?

**What Free Ventures is.** Berkeley's student-run startup accelerator. You apply *with* your startup — it's not a club you join and then find a project, it's a cohort you enter with something you're already building. Accepted teams get a structured program: mentorship, a curriculum of sorts, connections into the Berkeley and Bay Area startup ecosystem, and a demo day at the end of the semester. Some cohorts have come with a small amount of funding attached, though you should verify the current terms rather than assume.

**Why it's your priority one, restated so it's explicit.** Every other club on this list asks you to spend hours on something *other than* your startup. Free Ventures is the only one where the hours you spend are spent *on* the startup. The opportunity cost is near zero — it's the same work, with structure, deadlines, and people who've done it before looking over your shoulder. Nothing else on the list has that property.

**What they look for.** Roughly, in order:

1. *A team that's already building.* Not an idea, not a deck — evidence of shipping. You have a cofounder and something real, which puts you above most freshman applicants immediately.
2. *Traction, loosely defined.* Users, revenue, a working product, a pilot, a waitlist — any evidence someone outside the founding team cares. Even small numbers count if you can talk clearly about what they mean.
3. *Founder quality and coachability.* Can you explain what you're building without jargon, do you know why the hard part is hard, and do you update when someone pushes back.
4. *A reason the program specifically helps you.* Generic "we want mentorship" is weak. "We need intros to X kind of customer and we need someone to force us to ship by a date" is strong.

**Application components, typically:** written application with short answers (what you're building, why you, traction, what you need), a product link or demo, and then interview rounds for teams that advance — usually one screening conversation and one deeper session with partners where they pressure-test the business.

**The dates that constrain you.** Info session September 3. Applications close September 11. That's eight days between the info session and the deadline, in the first two weeks of your first semester, overlapping exactly with ML@B and Codebase recruiting. The application is not something to start on September 10.

**What you should be doing before September 3:** have a crisp one-paragraph description of the startup, a working demo link that doesn't require explanation, whatever traction numbers you have written down honestly, and a specific answer to "what do you need from us." All of that is startup work you should do regardless of whether Free Ventures accepts you, which makes it the cheapest possible preparation on this list.
That's useful. What's the actual semester commitment if I get in — is it on top of my 8-10 hours or does it come out of startup time?

Mostly out of startup time, which is the whole reason it's cheap.

**The fixed overhead:** a weekly cohort session (1-2 hrs), periodic mentor meetings you schedule yourself (1 hr every week or two), and demo day prep concentrated at the end. Call the pure overhead 3-4 hrs/week.

**The rest of the "commitment" is working on your own company** — the program expects progress between sessions, but that progress is your product, your customers, your fundraising. You were going to do that anyway. It's not additive time; it's the same time with accountability attached.

**So the honest accounting for your fall:**

- Free Ventures: ~3-4 hrs/week of genuinely new overhead
- Second club (ML@B): 8-10 hrs/week average, spiking to 15-20 for three weeks
- Second club (Codebase): steady 8-10, no light weeks
- Second club (Blueprint): 6-8, low variance

Against a stated 8-10 hr/week ceiling for clubs total, Free Ventures plus *any* of the three second options breaks your ceiling. Free Ventures plus Blueprint breaks it least. Free Ventures plus ML@B breaks it badly for about a month.

**Which surfaces the question you've been circling without asking directly:** is the 8-10 hr cap a real constraint or a comfort number? If it's real, the answer is Free Ventures plus Blueprint, or Free Ventures alone. If you'd revise it to 14-15 in exchange for something worth it, ML@B becomes viable. You should decide which of those is true before September, because you cannot decide it in the middle of an interview.

**One more thing worth saying plainly:** Free Ventures is competitive and you might not get in. The downside case — rejected from Free Ventures, rejected from ML@B — is real and you should have a plan for it that isn't "join nothing." That's a genuine argument for applying to Blueprint as a third application, even though it's the least on-target club, purely because the acceptance odds are different in kind.
What about the hackathon scene? People keep telling me that's where the actual builders are.

Partly true, and it's a genuinely different category from the four clubs above — different commitment shape, different value.

**Cal Hacks** is the big one: a large annual hackathon plus a year-round organizing team. Two distinct ways to engage:

*As a participant* — near-zero ongoing commitment. You show up for a weekend, build something, meet people. This is the highest-value-per-hour item on your entire list and it costs you nothing in recurring time. There is no reason not to do this.

*As an organizer* — a real club commitment, 5-10 hrs/week, spiking hard in the weeks before the event. The work is logistics, sponsorship, and operations, not building. It's valuable for a specific kind of person who wants to run large things and build relationships with sponsor companies. For you it's a poor fit: it consumes builder hours and produces organizer skills.

**The broader hackathon scene** around Berkeley includes AI-specific hackathons, sponsor-run events, and Bay Area events you can reach without much friction. As a participant, these are pure upside: weekend-shaped, no recurring obligation, high density of people who ship things, and occasionally a prize or a sponsor relationship that matters.

**How this changes your club math.** The hackathon scene gives you the thing you'd partly be joining ML@B or Codebase for — a technical peer group and forcing functions — at roughly a tenth of the recurring time cost. It doesn't give you the sustained project depth or the credential. But if your second-slot decision is close, the existence of a low-cost substitute for *some* of the value is a real argument for taking the lighter club and filling the gap with hackathons.

**Concretely:** put the major hackathon weekends on your calendar now, before your semester fills. They're the cheapest thing on this list and the easiest to lose to a scheduling conflict you could have avoided in August.

**Related and worth knowing about:** there are startup-adjacent orgs beyond Free Ventures — venture-scout style groups, entrepreneurship societies, and student-run funds. Most are more social and networking-shaped than building-shaped. Given you're already building, they're low priority, but I can go through them if you want the full map rather than the short list.
Yeah give me the full map of what else exists. I don't want to find out in November that there was an obvious fit I never heard of.

Reasonable. Here's the wider landscape, grouped by what they actually are, with a blunt fit call on each.

**Technical project orgs (same category as ML@B / Codebase / Blueprint)**

- *Launchpad-style accelerator-adjacent technical orgs* — build products with a startup framing rather than a client framing. Closer to your interests than Codebase, similar workload. Worth a look if it's recruiting.
- *Data Science Society* — projects, a curriculum, and industry-partner work. Broader and less selective than ML@B, technically shallower. Reasonable safety in the ML direction if ML@B rejects you.
- *Robotics and hardware orgs* — high commitment, high cohesion, off-target for you unless the startup touches hardware.

**Startup and venture orgs**

- *Free Ventures* — covered. Your priority one.
- *Student-run venture funds and scout programs* — you evaluate startups instead of building one. Good for network and for learning how investors think, which is directly useful when you fundraise. Time cost is usually modest, a few hours a week. The catch: most are selective and skew toward upperclassmen, and the work is analysis, not building.
- *Entrepreneurship societies and startup social clubs* — mixed quality. Some are genuine communities, some are resume lines with a speaker series. Evaluate individually by going to one event before committing to anything.
- *SkyDeck-adjacent programs* — Berkeley's accelerator ecosystem extends past student orgs. Not a club you join as a freshman, but worth knowing the landscape exists for later.

**AI-specific groups**

- The AI club scene has expanded a lot. Reading groups, safety-focused groups, applied-AI project groups. Quality varies enormously and several are new enough that reputation hasn't settled. The reading groups are usually low-commitment and high-signal — a good way to find people without joining anything.

**Consulting and business**

- *Berkeley Consulting* — you ruled it out. Correctly, by your own criteria.
- Other consulting and pre-professional business orgs share the same structure: intense social recruiting, deck-shaped work. Same rejection applies to all of them.

**Community and social**

- Cultural orgs, hobby clubs, intramural sports. These are not competing for the same slot and shouldn't be evaluated on the same axis. The relevant point: your 8-10 hr club budget is being spent entirely on *work-shaped* activities. That's a choice, and it's worth making it consciously rather than discovering in October that everything you do is a deliverable.

**The honest filter on all of this:** you already ran the right process. Builder-first, startup-adjacent, tight-knit, time-capped — that filter produces Free Ventures plus one of three, and nothing in this wider map beats what's already on your list. The main thing the wider map buys you is confidence that you're not missing an obvious fit, plus two safeties (Data Science Society, Blueprint) if the selective ones say no.
Let's do the actual time math. My fall schedule isn't final but assume a standard first-semester applied math load plus CS. Where does the club time actually come from?

Let's build the week from the bottom up rather than arguing about a club budget in the abstract.

**Fixed academic load.** A standard first semester for your track is four courses, one of which is a heavy math course and one of which is a heavy intro CS course, plus a breadth course and something lighter. Contact hours — lectures, discussions, labs — land around 15-17 hrs/week. Outside work for that load, honestly done, is another 18-25 hrs/week, front-loaded toward the CS course's project deadlines and the math course's problem sets. Call academics 35-40 hrs/week as a realistic band, with bad weeks at 45.

**Startup.** You said "genuinely limited" time for clubs because the startup exists. Whatever the startup currently takes — and you'd know better than me — it's the variable that moves most. If it's 15 hrs/week, your committed total is already 50-55.

**Sleep and non-negotiables.** 7-8 hrs/night is 50 hrs/week. Meals, commuting across a campus that is not small, laundry, and the basic overhead of being a person is another 15-20. That's 65-70 hrs/week you don't get to allocate.

**The arithmetic.** 168 hours in a week. Subtract 70 for the non-negotiables: 98 left. Subtract 38 for academics: 60. Subtract 15 for the startup: 45 hrs/week of genuinely discretionary time.

**45 sounds like a lot, and this is where the plan usually breaks.** That 45 is where friendships, exercise, the ability to say yes to something interesting on a Thursday, and recovery from bad weeks all live. Spending 10 of it on clubs is fine. Spending 20 means every unplanned thing — a sick week, a startup emergency, a midterm that goes badly — comes directly out of sleep, because there's no slack left.

**So the 8-10 hr cap isn't arbitrary and you shouldn't casually raise it.** It's roughly 20% of your discretionary time, which is a sane fraction for structured commitments in a first semester. The version of you in October who took ML@B *and* Free Ventures is running at 13-14 in a normal week and 20+ in the spike, which means the spike weeks are funded entirely by sleep and the startup.

**The uncomfortable implication.** If Free Ventures accepts you — 3-4 hrs of overhead on work you're already doing — you have 4-6 hrs of club budget left. That fits Blueprint (6-8, close enough) and does not fit ML@B or Codebase without revising the cap. That's not me telling you what to do; it's what your own numbers say.
Ugh, that's clarifying and annoying. But first semester is also when everyone says to over-commit and then cut. Is that wrong?

It's half right, and the half that's wrong is the expensive half.

**What's right about it:** you genuinely don't know what these clubs feel like from the outside, exploration is cheaper in the first semester than later, and dropping a club in week four costs you almost nothing socially. Trying things and cutting is a real strategy.

**What's wrong about it for your specific situation:**

*The clubs you're considering can't be cut cheaply.* "Over-commit then cut" works for clubs you can walk away from. ML@B places you on a project team of five people who are depending on you; Codebase puts you on a client deliverable. Leaving in October isn't a personal decision, it's a defection from a team — and the technical org community at Berkeley is small enough that this follows you. Blueprint is slightly more forgiving but the same structure applies.

*You can't re-apply cheaply either.* These orgs recruit once or twice a year in a narrow window. Cutting ML@B in October means your next shot is spring, or next fall. So "try it and cut" is really "consume a scarce application slot, then burn it."

*You already have the thing over-committing is supposed to teach you.* The advice exists because most freshmen don't know what they want and need data. You have an unusually specific filter already — builder-first, startup-adjacent, tight community, time-capped — and it's produced a clear ranking. You're not in the exploration regime; you're in the execution regime.

**The version of the advice that does apply to you:** over-commit on the *cheap* stuff. Go to five club info sessions in the first two weeks — that costs you six hours total and tells you more than any amount of reading. Do hackathons, which are weekend-shaped and free to skip. Attend one meeting of the AI reading groups. Say yes to things that don't create obligations to other people.

Be greedy about exploration where exit is free, and conservative where exit is expensive. Your list of four clubs is entirely in the expensive-exit category, which is exactly why you should decide before September rather than during it.
Ok that framing helps. Give me the actual fall calendar then — what happens when, so I can see the collisions.

Here's the shape of it. Treat specific dates other than the Free Ventures ones as approximate until you confirm at the activities fair.

**Late August — move-in and syllabus week.**
Everything feels easy. This is a trap: your academic load hasn't landed yet, so you'll overestimate your capacity in exactly the week you're making commitments. Whatever your calendar feels like in week one, it is wrong by about 15 hours.

**Week one — the activities fair.**
Every org in one place. Go, collect information, talk to actual members, and ask each one the same two questions: how many hours in your worst week, and what happens if I have to miss two weeks. The answers vary enormously and the difference between the official answer and the member answer is the most useful signal you'll get all fall.

**September 3 — Free Ventures info session.**
Your priority-one item. Go. Come with the startup description tight and a specific question, because being remembered by name before the application is read is worth more than anything you can put in the application itself.

**Early-to-mid September — the recruiting collision.**
ML@B, Codebase, Blueprint, and most other technical orgs run applications and interviews inside roughly the same two-week window. Expect: three to four written applications, two to four interviews, all during weeks two and three of the semester, while your first CS project and first math problem set are due.

**September 11 — Free Ventures applications close.**
Eight days after the info session. This is the hard deadline in your fall and everything else should schedule around it. Practically: the application should be substantially written before September 3 and revised after the info session, not started after it.

**Mid-to-late September — decisions.**
Most technical orgs release decisions before the end of the month. Free Ventures interview rounds run after the deadline, so you may be interviewing for Free Ventures while hearing back from the others. Order matters: try not to accept a heavy second club before you know the Free Ventures outcome.

**October — first project cycle, first midterms.**
The point where the semester's real load becomes visible. Whatever you committed to in September gets tested here, simultaneously with your first round of midterms. This is the month people discover their September self was optimistic.

**November — crunch.**
Project deadlines, client demos, second midterms, and if you're in Free Ventures, demo day prep. The peak-load month by a wide margin.

**The two collisions to design around:**
1. Free Ventures deadline versus technical org recruiting, both in the first three weeks. Solution: write the Free Ventures application in August.
2. Club project crunch versus midterms in October and November. Solution: pick the club whose spike doesn't align with yours, or pick the one without a spike.
That August point is the actionable one. What should I actually have done before I get to campus?

Short list, ordered by leverage. Most of it is startup work that pays off regardless of any club outcome.

**1. Write the Free Ventures application in August.** Not a draft — a real version. The short answers, the traction numbers, the demo link, the specific ask. You'll revise it after the September 3 info session, but revision takes an hour and writing from scratch during syllabus week takes a weekend you won't have. This is the single highest-leverage item on the list.

**2. Make the demo not require explanation.** Whatever your product is, someone should be able to open the link and understand it in thirty seconds without you narrating. This is the thing most student applications get wrong and it's fixable in a weekend.

**3. Write down your traction honestly.** Users, conversations, revenue, pilots, waitlist — whatever exists, with real numbers and real dates. Small honest numbers with a clear story beat vague large claims, and partners can tell the difference instantly. If the number is zero, the story is what you learned and what you shipped.

**4. Have the "what do you need from us" answer.** Specific: which kind of introductions, which decision you're stuck on, what deadline you want imposed. Generic answers about mentorship and networking are the default and read as such.

**5. Prep the technical interview surface, lightly.** A weekend of ML fundamentals if you're applying to ML@B, general data structures if Codebase. You're not starting from zero and you don't need a month. The bigger win is having a crisp two-minute story about something you built — which, again, you already have.

**6. Decide the cap question now.** Is 8-10 hrs/week real, or would you go to 14 for the right club. Decide it in August, in writing, when you're calm. If you leave it open you will decide it in an ML@B interview when someone asks about your commitment, and you will say yes.

**7. Put hackathon weekends on the calendar.** Cheapest item, easiest to lose to a conflict you could have avoided.

**8. Pick your second-club application set and stop researching.** You have enough information. More research past this point is procrastination with a productive costume on.

Everything above is doable in about two focused days spread across August. Items 1 through 4 are startup work that has value even if every club rejects you, which makes them unambiguously worth doing first.
Makes sense. One thing I keep going back and forth on — am I underrating the network effects of a club like ML@B? Everyone frames it as a long-term asset.

You're probably rating it correctly and being told to rate it higher by people whose situation is different from yours.

**The network argument in its strongest form:** technical orgs concentrate talented people, and the relationships compound. Alumni are at good companies and become useful five years out. The person on your project team becomes a cofounder, an early hire, or the reason you get a meeting. That is real, and it's the honest core of why people rank these clubs highly.

**Three reasons it's weaker for you than for the median member.**

*You already have the primary asset the network is a substitute for.* For most students, the club network is how they get access to opportunities — internships, referrals, a first job. You're building a company. Your access path runs through customers, investors, and the startup ecosystem, and Free Ventures plugs into that directly. The ML@B network is a strong second-best path to a place you're already walking toward by a first-best one.

*Network value is not proportional to hours.* The relationships that matter come from a handful of people you actually work closely with, not from org membership. You can get a meaningful fraction of that from hackathons, from reading groups, from being the person who ships things, and from Free Ventures' own cohort — which is, notably, a network of *founders*, which is more targeted to your situation than a network of strong engineers.

*The compounding argument has a time horizon problem.* "Useful in five years" is a real benefit, but you're spending hours in a semester where those hours have an unusually high alternative use, because early startup time compounds too, and faster. If the startup works, the ML@B network was a nice-to-have. If it doesn't, you'll have three more years to join things — and you'll be a stronger applicant then, having built something.

**Where the counter-argument is right:** if you get into Free Ventures and the startup then dies in November, you'd have zero clubs and a network of exactly one cofounder. That's a real downside scenario and it's the best argument for taking a second club. But note the argument is about *insurance*, not about network compounding — and if it's insurance you want, Blueprint at 6-8 predictable hours is a much better insurance product than ML@B at 8-20.

**The clean way to hold both:** ML@B's network is real and you are correctly discounting it, because your counterfactual is unusually strong. Just don't discount it to zero out of motivated reasoning about the workload.
Alright, do the head-to-head for slot two. ML@B vs Codebase vs Blueprint, on my actual criteria, and don't hedge.

Scoring against your four stated criteria: builder-first, startup-adjacent, tight community, fits the time cap.

**Builder-first (does it make you a better builder)**
- ML@B: strongest. Projects can fail, which is where learning lives. Pushes you past your current ceiling in a direction — ML systems — that you don't currently get from coursework or the startup.
- Codebase: middling. Excellent engineering practice, but it's practice at something you already do daily. Marginal skill gain is small for you specifically.
- Blueprint: weakest. CRUD-shaped work below your current level. The skill it does add — building for non-technical users — is real but narrow.

**Startup-adjacent (does it connect to what you're building)**
- ML@B: indirect. Technical credibility and ML capability that may matter to your product, plus a peer group that includes future founders.
- Codebase: indirect. Client work resembles agency work more than startup work. The connection is people, not substance.
- Blueprint: weakest. Nonprofit software is a different world entirely.
- None of the three beat Free Ventures on this axis by an order of magnitude, which is precisely why Free Ventures is priority one and this whole comparison is for a secondary slot.

**Tight community**
- Blueprint: strongest, clearly. Warmest culture, most patient, most social cohesion.
- Codebase: strong. Well-run, genuinely friendly, real social layer.
- ML@B: good but more intense and more competitive. Community as a byproduct of shared difficulty rather than as a cultivated thing.

**Time cap**
- Blueprint: fits at 6-8 with low variance.
- Codebase: at the ceiling, 8-10, no light weeks, and inflexible because a client depends on you.
- ML@B: breaks it. 8-10 average, 15-20 for three weeks, plus 3-4 hrs of first-semester education track. Realistically 12-14 average in your first semester.

**The honest ranking, and it splits by which question you're really asking.**

*If the 8-10 cap is real:* **Blueprint.** It's the only one that fits, it's the strongest on community, and the technical gap is partly filled by hackathons and by the startup itself. This is the answer your own numbers produce.

*If you'd revise the cap to 13-14 for something worth it:* **ML@B.** It's the only one of the three that clearly gives you something you can't get elsewhere. If you're going to break your time budget, break it for the option with the highest ceiling, not for the middle one.

*Codebase is dominated in both scenarios.* At the cap it loses to Blueprint on both hours and community; above the cap it loses to ML@B on learning. It's an excellent club that happens to sit in the exact spot where your particular circumstances give it nothing to win on. Cut it from consideration and reclaim the application slot.

**So the real decision is not three-way. It's: is the cap real?** Answer that and slot two answers itself.
Cutting Codebase feels right actually. So it's Blueprint vs ML@B, gated on the cap question. What's the opportunity cost of each in concrete terms?

Framed as what you give up, not what you get.

**If you take ML@B (assume ~13 hrs/week average, 18+ in the November spike):**

- You spend roughly 3-4 more hours per week than the cap, which comes out of the 45 discretionary hours. In a normal week that's fine. In a bad week — sick, midterm, startup emergency — you have no slack, and the deficit gets paid in sleep.
- The November spike collides with midterms and, if you're in Free Ventures, with demo day prep. That's the single worst three-week window in your fall and ML@B makes it materially worse.
- Startup velocity drops. Not to zero, but noticeably, in the semester where your cofounder is presumably also adjusting to a new schedule. If Free Ventures accepted you partly on momentum, this is the semester you'd be spending that momentum.
- You give up flexibility to say yes to unplanned things — a hackathon that appears with two weeks' notice, a customer who wants to talk on a Saturday, a conference.
- What you buy: the strongest technical peer group available to you, real ML depth, and a credential with weight.

**If you take Blueprint (~7 hrs/week, low variance):**

- You stay inside the cap with a few hours of margin, which is the difference between a plan that survives contact with October and one that doesn't.
- You give up the technical stretch. Realistically you will be the strongest engineer on your team, which is comfortable and not very educational.
- You give up the ML@B credential and peer group. Partially replaceable via hackathons and reading groups, not fully.
- You may be frustrated by the pace — waiting on nonprofit stakeholders is a real and commonly cited annoyance for people coming from faster environments.
- What you buy: a genuine community, a functioning first semester, preserved startup velocity, and slack for the unplanned.

**The asymmetry worth noticing.** ML@B's downside is concentrated in a specific, predictable, three-week window that you can see coming. Blueprint's downside is diffuse — mild under-stimulation across fourteen weeks. People systematically underrate the diffuse cost and overrate the acute one, because the acute one is vivid. Correct for that.

**The other asymmetry, cutting the other way.** You can join Blueprint next fall. It recruits every semester with a high acceptance rate and it will still be there. ML@B is harder to get into and you're strongest as an applicant when you have momentum from a project — which you have right now. Scarcity favors taking the harder-to-get option when it's offered.

**My read, which you should discount appropriately:** if Free Ventures accepts you, take Blueprint or nothing — the Free Ventures plus startup combination is already a full plate and ML@B on top is the plan that breaks in November. If Free Ventures rejects you, take ML@B — you'll have the hours, and you'll want the peer group more than ever.

Last few things. What exactly should I ask people at the activities fair — you said the member answer differs from the official answer.

The official answer is on the flyer. These questions get you the member answer.

**1. "What did your worst week last semester look like, in hours?"**
Not the average — the average is marketing. The worst week is the constraint. Watch for the pause before the number; a long pause means the number is higher than what they say. Follow up with "how many weeks like that were there?"

**2. "What happens if I have to miss two weeks?"**
This tests the club's flexibility, which is the variable you actually care about given an unpredictable startup. Answers range from "you'd tell your team and it's fine" to visible discomfort. The discomfort is the signal.

**3. "What's the thing people complain about?"**
Every org has one. If they say "nothing," they're either new or performing. Real answers — the education track is tedious, the client went dark for a month, the project scope was set by someone who left — tell you more than any amount of positive description.

**4. "Who did you actually get close to, and how?"**
Tests whether the community is structural or incidental. "My project team, we were in the lab until 2am" is a different club from "I know everyone's name."

**5. "What did you build, and what was hard about it?"**
This is a technical-depth probe disguised as a friendly question. If a member can't articulate what was hard, the projects aren't hard. If they light up and go into detail, that's the club that will stretch you.

**6. "What do you wish you'd known before joining?"**
The catch-all. Usually produces the most honest sentence of the conversation.

**7. For Free Ventures specifically: "What separated the teams that got in from the ones that didn't?"**
Ask this at the September 3 info session, to a partner, not a general member. It's the highest-value question you can ask that day and most people won't ask it.

**Two meta-notes.** Ask the same questions at every table so the answers are comparable — the variance between orgs on question 2 alone will sort your list. And talk to a second-year member rather than a first-year: first-years are still in the honeymoon and organizers are selling.
Good. What about the Free Ventures interview itself — what should I expect and where do teams usually blow it?

Expect two things: a screening conversation, then a deeper session with partners for teams that advance. The screening is largely "is this real and are these people serious." The deeper one is where it's decided.

**What they're actually testing.**

*Is the problem real.* Can you describe a specific person with a specific problem, and evidence that the problem hurts. Not a market size — a person.

*Do you understand why it's hard.* Every startup has a hard part. If you describe your business as straightforward, either you haven't found the hard part or you're hiding it, and both read badly.

*Are you actually shipping.* Cadence matters more than magnitude. "We've shipped every week since May and here's what changed" is stronger than one impressive-sounding launch.

*Do you update.* They will push back on something. The test is not whether you defend it — it's whether you distinguish between pushback that's right and pushback that's wrong, and say so directly. Caving on everything reads as no conviction; defending everything reads as uncoachable.

*Is the cofounder relationship sound.* If you're both in the room, they're watching how you handle disagreement in front of strangers. Deferring to each other unnaturally is worse than a visible, well-handled difference of opinion.

**Where teams blow it, in rough order of frequency.**

1. *Pitching the vision instead of the state.* Twenty minutes on what the company becomes in five years, nothing on what exists today. Partners have heard a thousand visions. State — what's built, who uses it, what you learned last week — is scarce and credible.
2. *Vague traction.* "A lot of interest," "several conversations," "strong signal." These are read as zero, correctly. A real number, even a small one, with a date and a story, is dramatically stronger.
3. *No specific ask.* "We want mentorship and networking" is the default answer and it signals you haven't thought about what you're stuck on.
4. *Not knowing your own numbers.* If you can't answer how many users, how much revenue, what your retention looks like, without checking — the impression is that you don't look at them, which is worse than the numbers being bad.
5. *Being defensive about the weak part.* Every early startup has an obvious hole. Naming it yourself, and saying what you'd need to learn to close it, converts your biggest liability into evidence of self-awareness. Waiting for them to find it converts it into a doubt about your judgment.
6. *Freshman apology.* Volunteering that you're new, that it's early, that you're still figuring it out. They know your year. Let the work speak.

**One structural advantage you have.** Most freshman applicants apply with an idea and a deck. You're applying with a cofounder and a thing that exists. That is a large gap and you should not talk yourself down out of it — but you also shouldn't lean on it. The gap is your floor, not your pitch.
What if they ask why I'm applying as a freshman when I could wait until I have more traction?

Good question to have an answer for, because a version of it will come up.

**The wrong answers.** "Why not" — reads as unserious. "To learn" — everyone says it. Anything that treats the program as a credential rather than a tool.

**The structure of a strong answer.** Say what you're stuck on, say why the program specifically unblocks it, and say what happens on the timeline if you wait.

Concretely, the shape is: *"We're not blocked on building — we ship weekly. We're blocked on [specific thing: reaching a category of user, deciding between two directions, knowing whether to charge]. That's a problem where an outside forcing function and people who've made the same call are worth more to us than another three months of iterating alone. And waiting a semester costs us the semester — the version of us that applies in spring is the version that spent fall guessing."*

That answer does three things: it demonstrates you're shipping, it shows you know your specific constraint, and it makes the timing argument concrete rather than eager.

**The honest sub-answer if they push on maturity.** You can name it directly: you're a freshman, you have less experience than most of the cohort, and what you bring instead is time, an existing product, and a cofounder relationship that already survived building something. That's a trade they can evaluate. Naming the weakness and pricing it is stronger than pretending it isn't there.

**One thing to avoid entirely:** don't say you'll apply again in spring if this doesn't work out. It's true and it's fine to think, but saying it in the room lowers the stakes of the decision for the person making it.
Ok. Last thing — what does this look like beyond freshman fall? Am I setting myself up well for spring and sophomore year, or optimizing myself into a corner?

You're setting up well, with one risk worth naming.

**Why the setup is good.**

*The plan is reversible.* Nothing in the tree commits you past December. Blueprint can be left after a semester without much cost. Free Ventures is cohort-shaped and ends. ML@B is the only sticky one and it's conditional. You've built a plan with cheap exits, which is the right property for a first semester.

*You're accumulating the right kind of evidence.* A semester of shipping plus whatever Free Ventures adds makes you a stronger applicant to everything in spring — including ML@B, which is easier to get into with a real project behind you. The plan compounds regardless of which branch fires.

*You're protecting the scarce thing.* Startup momentum in the first year is genuinely scarce; club membership is not. You've allocated correctly.

**What spring looks like on each branch.**

If Free Ventures accepted you: spring is either a second Free Ventures-adjacent semester, or the startup has grown enough that clubs are irrelevant and you should say so plainly. Either way you'll have a demo day behind you and a much clearer picture of whether the company is real.

If Free Ventures rejected you: re-apply in spring with a fall's worth of traction. Rejection at the freshman-fall stage is usually about stage rather than about you, and the spring application from someone who kept shipping is a different application.

If everything rejected you: spring is the easy semester to join things — recruiting is less competitive, you know the campus, and you have a fall of evidence. This branch feels bad in September and is close to costless by February.

**Sophomore year** is where the leverage shows up. If the startup is working, clubs become optional and you'll want the time back. If it isn't, you'll have a year of building behind you, which makes you a strong candidate for anything technical and — more importantly — you'll know a lot more about what you actually want than any amount of freshman-year research could tell you.

**The one real risk: optimizing entirely around the startup.**
Every item in this plan is work-shaped. Free Ventures is work. ML@B and Blueprint are work. Hackathons are work you enjoy. The failure mode isn't burnout in the dramatic sense — it's arriving at May having spent nine months exclusively with people who are useful to you, and having built no relationships that exist for no reason.

That matters instrumentally as well as personally: founders who only know other founders develop narrow judgment, and the friend who has nothing to do with your company is the one who tells you the truth about it.

**Cheap mitigation, worth doing:** one non-work commitment — a sport, a cultural org, a hobby club, anything where the point is the thing itself. Two to three hours a week, outside the club budget, and hold it as firmly as you'd hold a client deadline. It's the one line item in this plan you'll be tempted to cut first and should cut last.
Before the final save — help me with how to describe the startup itself. I keep either underselling it or making it sound like vaporware.

That oscillation is the standard failure and it has a structural cause: you're switching between describing the *vision* (sounds like vaporware) and describing the *implementation* (sounds small). The fix is to describe the **change in the world for one user**, which is neither.

**The three-layer structure that works:**

*Layer 1 — the concrete situation, one sentence.* Who, doing what, and what goes wrong. No product yet. "A [specific person] trying to [specific task] currently has to [painful thing]." If a listener can't picture a real person here, nothing after this lands.

*Layer 2 — what you built, one sentence.* What it does, mechanically. Not the philosophy of it. Someone should be able to repeat this sentence to a third party accurately.

*Layer 3 — the evidence, one or two sentences.* What happened when a real person used it. Numbers if you have them, a specific anecdote if you don't. "Ten people signed up" is fine. "One person used it four times last week and told us why" is often better, because it's harder to fake and it implies you talked to them.

**Then stop.** The vision goes at the end, in one sentence, only if asked. Vision first is what makes it sound like vaporware; vision as a footnote to demonstrated reality is what makes it sound inevitable.

**On underselling.** The two habits that cause it are hedging language and comparative framing. Hedging — "it's kind of like," "just a small thing," "we're still figuring out" — you can simply delete; nothing is lost. Comparative framing — "it's a simpler version of [big company]" — is worse, because it anchors the listener on someone else's product and makes yours the diminished copy. Describe what yours does; let them make the comparison if they want it.

**The calibration test.** Say your description to someone outside the space. If they ask "so what does it actually do," layer 2 failed. If they ask "who would use that," layer 1 failed. If they nod politely and change the subject, layer 3 failed. Run this three or four times in August with different people and rewrite between each; four iterations will get you further than four hours of solo editing.

**One specific to the Free Ventures context:** the person across the table has heard hundreds of these. They aren't evaluating polish — they're checking whether the description has *load-bearing specifics* in it. Every replaceable noun in your pitch, every "users" that could be any user and every "problem" that could be any problem, is a spot where they conclude you haven't talked to anyone. Specificity reads as evidence, not as narrowness.
Related — how do they look at a two-person freshman team? Is the cofounder thing an asset or do they worry it falls apart?

Both, and which one dominates depends on what you can show about the relationship rather than about the product.

**Why it's an asset.** Solo founders are the more common failure mode at this stage — no one to argue with, no one to cover the gap in your skills, no one whose disappointment keeps you working in February. A functioning two-person team is genuinely rarer than a good idea, and programs know it. Two people who have already built something together have passed a test that most applicants haven't taken.

**Why they worry.** Freshman cofounder pairs dissolve at a high rate, and for predictable reasons: one person's interests shift after a semester of new classes, the workload splits unevenly and resentment accumulates quietly, or the relationship was formed on enthusiasm rather than on having survived a disagreement. From the outside, a pair that's been building for a few months and a pair that's been enthusiastic for a few months look identical.

**What distinguishes you, and what to make legible:**

*Duration under stress.* Not "we've worked together for six months" — "we disagreed about [X] in April, here's how we resolved it, here's what the resolution changed." One concrete disagreement, well described, does more than any amount of asserting that you work well together.

*Complementarity that's real.* If you both do the same thing, say so honestly and say how you divide it. Fake complementarity — assigning one of you a title neither of you does the work of — is transparent and costly.

*An explicit split.* Equity, decision rights, what happens if one of you wants out. Most freshman teams have not discussed this, and the ones that have signal seriousness immediately. You don't need paperwork; you need to have had the conversation and be able to describe its conclusion without looking at each other first.

*Independent capability.* Can each of you describe the whole product, including the part you didn't build? A team where one person can only speak to their half is a team with a bus problem.

**The thing to prepare for.** They may ask what happens if one of you gets a strong internship offer, or if the workload becomes unsustainable in November. The good answer is not "that won't happen." It's that you've discussed it, and here's what you agreed. Having *any* considered answer puts you ahead of most of the pool.

**And the honest framing if you're both in the room:** don't perform agreement. Interviewers watch for the pair that finishes each other's sentences too smoothly, because it usually means one person is doing the thinking. A visible, respectful difference of opinion — handled in ten seconds — is a stronger signal than uniformity.
Good. And how do I keep the startup from stalling during the September application crunch — three applications, interviews, and syllabus week all at once?

By deciding now what the startup's September looks like, at a deliberately reduced level, instead of letting it get squeezed unplanned.

**The failure mode you're avoiding.** September doesn't kill startups by taking all the time — it kills them by taking the *initiative*. You keep answering emails and fixing bugs, so it feels alive, but nothing new ships for five weeks. Then in October you've lost the thread, the momentum argument in your Free Ventures interview is stale, and restarting costs more than continuing would have.

**Set a floor, not a target.** Pick the smallest cadence that preserves momentum and treat it as non-negotiable: one shipped change per week, however small, plus one customer conversation per week. That's maybe 5-6 hrs. Everything above the floor is optional in September. A floor you actually hit for five weeks beats an ambitious plan you abandon in week two.

**Front-load the application work into August.** This is the same point as before but it's the main lever here: every hour of application writing you move into August is an hour that doesn't compete with shipping in September. The Free Ventures application, the ML@B and Blueprint applications, and your two-minute project story are all writable now.

**Batch the interviews.** When scheduling, cluster them into as few days as possible rather than spreading them across two weeks. Three interviews on two afternoons costs you two afternoons. The same three spread over ten days costs you ten days, because each one occupies the day around it.

**Protect one real block per week.** A single four-hour uninterrupted block does more than eight scattered hours, and it's the first casualty of a fragmented schedule. Put it on the calendar in August, before classes and clubs fill in around it, and defend it.

**Tell your cofounder the plan explicitly.** The most common September failure in two-person teams is one person quietly going dark on applications while the other assumes the usual pace and gets frustrated. Say: here are my three weeks, here's the reduced floor I'm committing to, here's what I need you to own. Ten minutes of that conversation in August prevents the resentment version of October.

**And use the application work.** Writing the Free Ventures application forces you to articulate the problem, the traction, and the specific thing you're stuck on. That's genuinely useful strategic work you'd otherwise defer indefinitely. Do it as a founding-team exercise with your cofounder rather than as paperwork, and September's biggest time sink becomes the clearest thinking you'll do all fall.
One more. If I only get into Free Ventures and nothing else, how do I replace the technical peer group I'd have gotten from ML@B? I don't want to spend the year only talking to my cofounder.

This is the right thing to be worried about in that branch, and it's solvable — but only if you treat it as a deliberate project rather than assuming it happens by proximity.

**Start with why it doesn't happen by default.** In a club, the peer group is manufactured for you: a fixed team, a shared deadline, a room you're in every week. Without that structure, you get the university's default social sorting — dorm floor, lecture halls, whoever sits near you — which is random with respect to the thing you care about. Berkeley is large enough that "I'll meet people naturally" produces a group with no particular relationship to building.

**Four substitutes, roughly in order of value per hour.**

*1. Hackathons, treated seriously rather than casually.* The highest-density concentration of builders you'll have access to, and it costs weekends rather than semesters. But the default hackathon experience — team up with people you already know, build, leave — produces almost no new relationships. Do the opposite: go without a team at least twice, join strangers, and get contact details from the two people whose work impressed you. Three hackathons done this way will produce more useful contacts than a semester of club meetings, because everyone there is self-selected for shipping.

*2. Reading groups and seminars.* Low commitment, high signal, and self-selecting for people who care about the material rather than the credential. The AI reading groups in particular tend to attract exactly the population ML@B does, minus the application process. Two hours a week, no obligations, and you can leave silently if the group is bad. Try three, keep one.

*3. Office hours and hard courses, used socially.* The people who stay after the hard CS course's office hours are a filtered population, and you'll be in the room anyway. This is free — it costs zero marginal hours because you're already there — and it's the substitute people most consistently overlook. The study group that forms around a difficult course is functionally a project team with a shared deadline; that's the same structure that makes club peer groups work.

*4. The Free Ventures cohort itself.* Worth naming explicitly, because in this branch it's your primary peer group and it's better targeted than ML@B would have been. These are founders — people making the same category of decision you are, on the same timeline, with the same specific problems. They're less useful for going deep on ML systems and more useful for everything else. Invest in them deliberately: the cohort relationships that persist are the ones where someone made the effort outside the scheduled sessions.

**The thing that actually determines whether this works.** Peer groups form around *repeated involuntary contact plus a shared difficulty*. Clubs manufacture both. Every substitute above is weaker on repetition — you see hackathon people once, reading group people weekly-but-passively. So you have to supply the repetition manually: follow up with specific people, propose a second interaction with a concrete reason, and be the one who organizes rather than the one who attends. That's maybe two hours a month of unglamorous effort and it's the entire difference between "I met some people" and "I have a group."

**A concrete version, since vague social advice is useless.** By the end of October in this branch you should have: three hackathons attended, one reading group you attend consistently, one study group from your hardest course, and two people from the Free Ventures cohort you've talked to outside a scheduled session. That's a checklist, not a vibe, and it's achievable inside 4-5 hrs/month on top of the plan you already have.

**And the honest caveat.** This is a real substitute for the *network* value of ML@B and a partial substitute for the *technical stretch* value. It does not replace being on a team where the project might fail and five people are depending on you — that specific pressure is hard to buy outside a structured org. If after a semester you find you miss that specifically, that's exactly the signal to apply to ML@B in spring, with a fall of evidence behind you.
